title: Compound sentences, くれる, あげる and the て-form
summary: The て-form links clauses into one long sentence with a single tense at the end, and くれる / あげる describe giving and doing something for someone.

blocks.text: Until now each sentence has been a single train. Real Japanese chains them. This lesson shows how, with a little story: a cat sits by a river while her big sister reads and ignores her.

A **position noun** like そば (beside) or 上 (top) works like any noun, so the place takes **に**: 川のそばにいる. And ある, "to exist", turns into a describing word in front of a noun: ある日 is "a certain day" ("one day") and ある本 is "a certain book".

blocks.jp: ある日、猫は川のそばにいた。
blocks.en: One day the cat was beside the river.

blocks.text: A verb in **て-form** that is not the last word says: this clause is finished, and **more is coming**. Tense is marked **only once, at the very end**, and it covers the whole sentence. So 読んでいて on its own could be "is reading" or "was reading" until the final past marker settles it.
Two clauses, one tense at the end.

blocks.jp: 姉は本を読んでいて、遊んでくれなかった。
blocks.en: My sister was reading a book and did not play with me.

blocks.text: くれる and あげる: giving

Both mean "give", and the difference is direction. In Japanese you always place yourself **below** other people. **くれる** is giving **down to me or my group**; **あげる** is giving **up and out to someone else**.

blocks.jp: 友達が私に本をくれた。
blocks.en: A friend gave me a book.

blocks.jp: 私は友達にプレゼントをあげた。
blocks.en: I gave my friend a present.

blocks.text: Put either after a **て-form verb** and it means doing the action **for someone's benefit**: 〜てくれる (someone does it for me), 〜てあげる (I do it for someone).

blocks.jp: 友達が宿題を手伝ってくれた。
blocks.en: A friend helped me with my homework.

blocks.jp: 弟に宿題を手伝ってあげた。
blocks.en: I helped my little brother with his homework.

items: **て-form** = "this clause is done, more follows". The **tense is marked once**, at the end.
**くれる**: giving **to me / my group**. **あげる**: giving **to someone else**.
**〜てくれる / 〜てあげる**: doing something **for** someone.
**ある日** = "one day"; position nouns take **に** (**川のそばに**).

questions.instruction: What does a て-form in the middle of a sentence tell you?
options: This clause is finished and more follows
The action is in the past
questions.note: て links clauses; the final verb carries the tense.

questions.instruction: Which says a friend gave ME a book?
options: 友達が私に本をくれた
友達が私に本をあげた
私が友達に本をくれた
questions.note: Giving toward me or my group is くれる.

questions.instruction: Which says I gave a friend a present?
options: 私は友達にプレゼントをあげた
私は友達にプレゼントをくれた
友達は私にプレゼントをあげた
私は友達にプレゼントがあげた
questions.note: Giving out to someone else is あげる.

questions.instruction: Tap the verb that carries the tense of the whole sentence
questions.note: Only the last verb is marked for tense.

questions.prompt: A friend helped me with my homework.
questions.note: て-form + くれた = did it for me.

questions.instruction: What does ある mean in ある日?
questions.note: ある in front of a noun means "a certain".

questions.instruction: Which particle marks the place in 川のそば＿＿いた?
questions.note: Position nouns are nouns: they take に.

questions.prompt: In a long て-chain, every verb carries its own tense.
questions.note: The tense is marked only once, at the end.
弟に宿題を手伝ってあげた.

questions.instruction: Why can 読んでいて be "is reading" or "was reading"?
options: Tense is decided by the verb at the end of the sentence
Because て is a past marker
Because いる has no tense
questions.note: て-form verbs carry no tense of their own.

questions.instruction: Which one means "My sister did not play with me"?
options: 姉は遊んでくれなかった
姉は遊んであげなかった
姉は遊ばなかったあげる
questions.note: The sister's action goes toward me, so くれる; negative past: くれなかった.

questions.instruction: Which pairs the verb with the right giving word?
questions.prompt: "I carried my grandmother's bag for her."
options: おばあちゃんの荷物を持ってあげた
おばあちゃんの荷物を持ってくれた
おばあちゃんの荷物を持ってもらった
おばあちゃんの荷物を持っていた
questions.note: I did it for someone else: 〜てあげる.
